About 16 min read · PDF pages 4–17 · Short version (Concise)

Learning goals

  • Translate a vague managerial request into a stakeholder, a decision, an action horizon, a KPI, a target, a guardrail and a bounded question.

  • Distinguish a KPI, a management target and a guardrail, and explain why passing one does not answer the question asked by another.

  • Calculate counts, proportions and target gaps, and report a gap between two rates in percentage points rather than as a percent change.

Decision-First Analysis and the MetroMeal Brief

Concept

What Decision-First Analysis Means

Decision-first analysis means defining the decision before touching the data. Name the stakeholder (the person who will act), the decision (the realistic choice), the action horizon (when the choice must be made), the outcome that matters and the evidence needed. A KPI, or key performance indicator, is a quantified measure used to monitor an objective and support that decision. A KPI informs a decision; it is not the decision. Starting here prevents a polished chart that answers a question nobody asked. If the stakeholder cannot name an action the evidence could change, clarify the decision first.

Concept

How the Frame Works: Who, What, and How

The session builds the frame with Who, What, and How: who will use the communication, what they need to know or do, and how the evidence will be delivered, live or in a document read without a presenter. The frame also separates two periods. The observed window is when the records were collected; the action horizon is when the decision takes effect. Data from the first cannot by themselves describe the second. Finally, draft a provisional claim before choosing a chart, and mark the words that need data support and the words that would imply a cause.

🧮 Worked example

Worked Evidence: Framing the MetroMeal Delivery Case

MetroMeal Delivery is the session's hypothetical running case. You are the operations analyst supporting the regional operations director, and the problem is a possible decline in on-time delivery. The vague request "Show whether delivery performance is getting worse" becomes: "Should the regional operations director investigate and potentially adjust weekend staffing for the next scheduling cycle, given weekly on-time delivery performance relative to the 85% target and the 3% complaint-rate guardrail?" The data hold one row per eligible completed delivery, August 3 through August 30, 2026: 2,000 rows, 500 per week. Constraints are a fixed staffing budget, customer privacy, incomplete causal information and protecting complaint performance.

Worked evidence

Population: Eligible completed MetroMeal deliveries (hypothetical teaching case)

Period: August 3 through August 30, 2026

Unit: Decision-frame elements

Frame element MetroMeal answer
Stakeholder Regional operations director
Decision Whether to investigate and potentially adjust weekend staffing
Action horizon Before the next scheduling cycle
KPI Weekly on-time delivery rate
Target At least 85.0% on time
Guardrail Complaint rate no greater than 3.0%
Evidence boundary Four descriptive weeks; no evidence that isolates a cause

Interpretation: The frame names who acts, what they may do and by when, before any rate or chart is produced.

Concept

Interpreting the Frame

The frame shows what the analysis can and cannot do. It can show whether the weekly on-time rate met the 85.0% target and whether complaints stayed within 3.0%. It can support a decision to investigate weekend staffing before the next cycle. It cannot show that staffing caused any change, because the records are observational and descriptive: they record what happened, not why. Weather, restaurant delays, order mix or staffing could each be involved, and nothing in the case separates them. That is why the frame says "investigate" rather than "fix".

⚠️ Common mistake

Common Misconception: The Chart Is the Deliverable

A widespread error is treating the chart as the product. Given "Show whether delivery performance is getting worse," an analyst produces a dramatic bar chart. But "getting worse" compares periods, and the request names no periods, deliveries or measure; different choices give different answers from the same records. A chart built without a decision also drifts toward the most striking pattern. The session's example draft, "Performance collapsed because staffing was inadequate," pairs an undefined dramatic word with a causal claim the data cannot support. The corrected sequence is decision, measure, records, calculation, chart, claim.

🚧 Limits and conditions

Limits of a Decision Frame

A frame improves focus but creates no evidence. A target is useful only when its owner, value, scope and effective period are known. The frame can also be wrong: if the director's real choice concerns weekday dispatch, a perfect weekend analysis misses the point, so confirm the decision with the stakeholder. Framing cannot fix the records either; whether the 500 weekly deliveries were recorded correctly is examined in Session 3. When data are observational and descriptive, frame the claim as what occurred in the observed window, not why it occurred.

🧭 Guided practice

Guided Practice: Framing the HarborCare Clinic Decision

HarborCare is a made-up clinic from Lab Part A; its numbers are not MetroMeal data. The clinic manager monitors the monthly no-show rate among eligible appointments, with a maximum of 10.0% no-shows and a complaint guardrail of 4.0%. One month shows 46 no-shows and 12 complaints among 400 eligible appointments. Task 1: Name the stakeholder, a decision limited to investigating or revising reminder scheduling, and the action horizon. Task 2: Calculate both rates and compare each with its own threshold. Task 3: Write one supported claim, one trend or causal claim to remove, and a revised question. Check: 46 ÷ 400 = 11.5%; 12 ÷ 400 = 3.0%.

Concept

The Rate Behind a KPI

rate=qualifying counteligible count,on-time rate=OE,complaint rate=CE \text{rate} = \frac{\text{qualifying count}}{\text{eligible count}}, \qquad \text{on-time rate} = \frac{O}{E}, \qquad \text{complaint rate} = \frac{C}{E}

Symbols and pronunciation

  • O O (say "oh"): number of eligible deliveries that met the promised-time rule

  • C C (say "see"): number of eligible deliveries with a recorded complaint

  • E E (say "ee"): number of eligible completed deliveries in the same week

Inputs and assumptions

Counts taken from the same eligible population and the same week. The numerator must be a subset of the denominator.

Worked steps

  1. Step 1: Count eligible completed deliveries for the week: E=500 E = 500 .

  2. Step 2: Count on-time deliveries among them: O=392 O = 392 ; count complaint deliveries among them: C=14 C = 14 .

  3. Step 3: Divide: 392/500=0.784 392 / 500 = 0.784 and 14/500=0.028 14 / 500 = 0.028 ; display as 78.4% and 2.8%.

Worked result

Week of August 24: on-time rate 78.4%; complaint rate 2.8%.

What the result means

Both rates share the 500-delivery denominator; the complaint rate is not 14 ÷ 392. The rate describes one week and says nothing yet about why 108 deliveries were late.

When to use it

When success relative to opportunity matters, or when the eligible total varies between periods.

Limits and conditions

Adding ineligible records, such as canceled or test orders, enlarges the denominator and understates the on-time share.

How to check the reference

Confirm 392 + 108 = 500, then divide 392 by 500 yourself instead of copying a dashboard value.

📖 Key terms

Key terms

Stakeholder: The person or role who will use the evidence to make a decision.
Decision-First Analysis: An approach that defines the stakeholder, choice, timing, outcome, comparison and evidence needs before selecting a measure or chart.
Action Horizon: The time by which a decision must be made or take effect.
Observed Window: The historical period in which the analyzed records were collected.
Key Performance Indicator (KPI): A quantified measure used to monitor an objective and support a decision.
✅ Study check

Put the learning into action

  • Rewrite a vague data request as a decision question that names the stakeholder, decision, time window, outcome, comparison, target and guardrail.

  • Use Who, What, and How to identify the audience, what it needs to do, and how the evidence will be delivered.

  • Draft a provisional claim before building a chart, and mark each word that needs data support or that implies a cause.

Counts, Proportions, and Percentage-Point Target Gaps

Concept

KPI, Target, and Guardrail as Separate Roles

Every MetroMeal number has one managerial role. The KPI is the monitored measure: the weekly on-time delivery rate. The target is the management benchmark: at least 85.0% on time. The guardrail is a second measure that should not deteriorate while the KPI is pursued: a complaint rate no greater than 3.0%. A target is chosen by management, not calculated from the records. The session's appendix adds that the 85.0% target is a minimum floor, so a miss should trigger an operational review, while the 3.0% guardrail is a maximum ceiling, so a breach should trigger customer-impact checks.

🔍 Go deeper

The Mechanism: Count, Proportion, and Target Gap

Three calculations turn records into KPI evidence. A count is a frequency, such as 392 on-time deliveries. A proportion divides the count by the eligible total. A target gap subtracts the target from the observed rate; when both are percentages, the direct difference is measured in percentage points. A negative gap means below target, not a negative rate. Percent change instead divides the difference by a baseline and describes relative size. Changing the baseline changes the percent change but not the percentage-point gap, so the session reports KPI gaps in points.

∑ Key equation

Worked Calculation: The Latest MetroMeal Week

For the week starting August 24, 2026, MetroMeal recorded 500 eligible completed deliveries: 392 on time and 108 late. First reconcile: 392 + 108 = 500. The on-time rate is 392 ÷ 500 = 78.4%, and the late rate is 108 ÷ 500 = 21.6%. The target gap is 78.4% − 85.0% = −6.6 percentage points. The guardrail is checked separately: 14 complaints ÷ 500 = 2.8%, within the 3.0% maximum.

Worked evidence

Population: Eligible completed MetroMeal deliveries, latest week

Period: August 24 through August 30, 2026

Unit: Deliveries and percentages

Quantity Calculation Result Benchmark Status
Denominator check 392 + 108 500 500 eligible Reconciles
On-time rate 392 ÷ 500 78.4% At least 85.0% Below target
Target gap 78.4 − 85.0 −6.6 points 0 or above Shortfall
Complaint rate 14 ÷ 500 2.8% At most 3.0% Within guardrail

Interpretation: The latest week missed the on-time target by 6.6 percentage points while complaints stayed inside their ceiling.

Concept

Interpreting a KPI Miss and a Guardrail Pass

Keep the two results separate. The KPI says 78.4% of 500 eligible deliveries in the latest week met the promised-time rule, 6.6 points below the 85.0% floor. The guardrail says complaints, at 2.8%, stayed below the 3.0% ceiling. Passing the guardrail does not cancel the KPI miss, because the measures answer different questions. Write the unit, population and week into every sentence: "78.4% of 500 eligible completed deliveries in the week of August 24 were on time." A bare "78.4%" invites readers to assume the wrong population, such as all customers.

⚠️ Common mistake

Common Misconception: Calling −6.6 a "6.6% Drop"

The most frequent error calls the gap "a 6.6% drop". The gap came from subtraction, so its unit is percentage points. Percent change divides by a baseline: (0.784 − 0.850) ÷ 0.850 × 100 = −7.76%, which the lab rounds to −7.8%. A second error reads the guardrail as good news about delivery: "The guardrail passed, so performance is fine." The two thresholds protect different outcomes. A third error uses the wrong complaint denominator: 14 ÷ 392 = 3.6%, which would falsely suggest a breach. Complaints are counted among all 500 eligible deliveries.

🚧 Limits and conditions

Limits of Counts, Proportions, and Gaps

These calculations describe one week well but have boundaries. A difference from target is not automatically statistically significant or managerially important; significance testing comes later in the course. One week shows a level, not a trend, because "worsening" compares periods. The on-time rate also hides severity, treating a delivery one minute late like one 50 minutes late, which is why Section 2.2 adds late-minute summaries. And a guardrail can miss harms: complaints may not capture excluded addresses, pressured couriers or customers who never complain.

Changed-Case Transfer: Percentage Points in a Different Setting

Apply the distinction to two session examples. First, the blog compares an observed 85.0% rate with a 90.0% target: calculate the gap in points and the relative shortfall. Second, the industry appendix reports an advertising-plan audience rising from 40 million to 70 million monthly active users: calculate the absolute increase and relative growth, and explain why "30 percentage points" is wrong. Check: −5.0 points and −5.56%; 30 million users and 75% growth.

Optional independent practice: my response

Write your approach, supporting evidence and assumptions here. After checking the explanation, record what you would revise.
Concept

Percentage-Point Gap and Percent Change

gappp=(r−T)×100,percent change=r−TT×100 \text{gap}_{pp} = (r - T) \times 100, \qquad \text{percent change} = \frac{r - T}{T} \times 100

Symbols and pronunciation

  • r r (say "ar"): observed rate, stored as a proportion such as 0.784

  • T T (say "tee"): target rate, stored as a proportion such as 0.85

  • gappp \text{gap}_{pp} (say "gap in percentage points"): direct difference between the two levels

Inputs and assumptions

Both rates are proportions of the same kind of event over comparable populations. The target is the baseline for percent change.

Worked steps

  1. Step 1: Subtract the target from the observed rate: 0.784−0.850=−0.066 0.784 - 0.850 = -0.066 .

  2. Step 2: Multiply by 100 for percentage points: −0.066×100=−6.6 -0.066 \times 100 = -6.6 .

  3. Step 3: For percent change, divide the difference by the target: −0.066/0.850=−0.0776 -0.066 / 0.850 = -0.0776 , or −7.76% -7.76\% .

Worked result

Gap = −6.6 percentage points; relative shortfall = −7.76% of the target level.

What the result means

Excel stores 78.4% as 0.784, so the lab formula =(B11-B8)*100 multiplies by 100 on purpose. If the cell shows −0.066, the multiplication is missing.

When to use it

Percentage points for a KPI's distance from target; percent change for relative growth from a named baseline.

Limits and conditions

Neither number says whether the gap is meaningful for the business or larger than normal week-to-week variation.

How to check the reference

Change the baseline to 0.876 and confirm that only the percent change moves.

📖 Key terms

Key terms

Target: A management benchmark or desired level for a KPI; it is chosen, not calculated from the records.
Guardrail: A measure that should not deteriorate while the primary KPI is pursued, with its own limit.
Count: The number of qualifying events, such as on-time deliveries.
Proportion: A qualifying count divided by an eligible total, ranging from 0 to 1 and often shown as a percentage.
Percentage Point: The unit of a direct difference between two percentages.
✅ Study check

Put the learning into action

  • Calculate a KPI rate and a guardrail rate from counts that share the same eligible denominator.

  • Report target gaps in percentage points and reserve percent change for relative comparisons with a named baseline.

  • Check the KPI and the guardrail separately, and report both results together.

Reference summary

Concept

Start With the Decision

Name the frame
  • Stakeholder, decision, action horizon, outcome, comparison and evidence come before any chart.
MetroMeal's frame
  • The regional operations director decides whether to investigate and potentially adjust weekend staffing before the next scheduling cycle.
Keep the boundary
  • Four descriptive weeks can support an investigation. They cannot show that staffing caused a result.
Concept

One Role per Number

KPI, target, guardrail
  • KPI: weekly on-time rate. Target: at least 85.0%. Guardrail: complaint rate at most 3.0%.
Floor and ceiling
  • The target is a minimum floor; the guardrail is a maximum ceiling. Higher on-time is better; lower complaints are better.
Concept

The Latest Week in Numbers

Reconcile, then divide
  • 392 on time + 108 late = 500 eligible. On-time rate: 392 ÷ 500 = 78.4%. Complaint rate: 14 ÷ 500 = 2.8%.
Report both results
  • The KPI missed its target; the guardrail stayed within its limit. One result does not cancel the other.
Concept

Points Versus Percent

Subtract for points
  • 78.4% − 85.0% = −6.6 percentage points.
Divide for percent change
  • −6.6 ÷ 85.0 = −7.76%. Name the baseline whenever you report a percent change.

Learning goals

Reproducible KPI Specification and Count-First Aggregation

Concept

What Makes a KPI Reproducible

A KPI is reproducible when another analyst could compute the same number from your written definition alone. A formula is not enough, because "on-time rate" can hide different populations, windows and rules. A KPI specification states the name, purpose, unit, eligible population, time window, grain, inclusion and exclusion rules, numerator or aggregation rule, denominator, direction of improvement, target, guardrail and refresh schedule. The eligible population is the set of records allowed into the denominator. Locking these rules before calculating means a later change in the number reflects operations, not a quiet change in definition.

Concept

How Aggregation From Counts Works

Count-first aggregation adds the qualifying counts across periods, adds the eligible counts, and divides once, so each delivery counts once. Averaging weekly percentages instead gives each week equal influence regardless of volume. A delivery-weighted rate asks what share of all eligible deliveries arrived on time; a week-weighted average asks what the average week looked like. They agree only when every week has the same denominator. The session's rule: do not average weekly percentages for an overall rate unless denominators are equal or an unweighted weekly average is explicitly the intended KPI.

🧮 Worked example

Worked Evidence: MetroMeal's Four Weeks

The lab rebuilds the weekly table from the 2,000 rows of orders_story.csv. Each week has 500 eligible deliveries, with 420, 438, 425 and 392 on time. Summing counts gives 1,675 of 2,000, or 83.75%, 1.25 points below target. Complaints total 47, a four-week rate of 2.35%. Averaging the four weekly rates also gives 83.75%, but only because the denominators are equal.

Worked evidence

Population: 2,000 eligible completed MetroMeal deliveries in orders_story.csv

Period: August 3 through August 30, 2026

Unit: Deliveries per week and percentages

Week start Eligible On time On-time rate Gap (points) Complaints Complaint rate
2026-08-03 500 420 84.0% −1.0 10 2.0%
2026-08-10 500 438 87.6% +2.6 11 2.2%
2026-08-17 500 425 85.0% 0.0 12 2.4%
2026-08-24 500 392 78.4% −6.6 14 2.8%
Four-week aggregate 2,000 1,675 83.75% −1.25 47 2.35%

Interpretation: Three weeks at or near target and one week well below it pool to 83.75%, so the total alone hides the weak latest week.

Concept

Interpreting the Weekly and Pooled Results

Read the table two ways. Down the rows, the latest week is the only one clearly below target, and its complaint rate is the highest of the four, though still within 3.0%. The aggregate row, 83.75%, is correct for all 2,000 deliveries but answers a different question: three strong weeks dilute the weak one. The director therefore needs the weekly rows, not only the total. Four weekly points describe a short sequence; they do not establish a stable trend or explain why the latest week was lower.

⚠️ Common mistake

Common Misconception: Averaging Rates Is Always Safe

Because MetroMeal's weeks are equal in size, =AVERAGE(...) of the weekly rates happens to give 83.75%. With unequal weeks it fails. The lab's example: 90 of 100 on time (90.0%) and 300 of 400 (75.0%) average to 82.5%, but only 390 of 500 deliveries were on time, 78.0%. A second misconception is that definitions can shift quietly. Adding abandoned calls to a resolution rate's denominator creates a new KPI version, and the session notes that if "on time" changed from 45 to 50 minutes, MetroMeal's rate could rise with no operational improvement.

🚧 Limits and conditions

Limits of Specifications and Pooled Rates

A specification makes a KPI repeatable, not correct: a wrongly assigned eligibility flag is repeated faithfully. A pooled rate hides timing, so 83.75% cannot show whether the shortfall was spread out or concentrated. Weighting is a choice that must follow the question. When a definition must change, version it: record the new rule, effective date, reason and approver, recalculate earlier results where the data allow, and warn users when comparisons break.

Task 3: Decide whether a count or a proportion answers the service question. Task 4: Write a one-line specification. Task 5: Explain how a changed eligibility rule could change the decision. Check: 90.0%; −2.0 points.

Changed-Case Transfer: A Larger Latest Week

The lab's optional Topic 5 changes one condition: MetroMeal's latest week becomes 784 on time out of 1,000 eligible, still 78.4%, with the first three weeks unchanged. Calculate the average of the four rates and the count-first rate, explain which counts every delivery once, and describe a situation in which a week-weighted average would be the intended KPI. Check: 83.75% versus 2,067 ÷ 2,500 = 82.68%.

Optional independent practice: my response

Write your approach, supporting evidence and assumptions here. After checking the explanation, record what you would revise.
Concept

Count-First Aggregation

Four-week rate=∑w=14Ow∑w=14Ewnot, in general,14∑w=14OwEw \text{Four-week rate} = \frac{\sum_{w=1}^{4} O_w}{\sum_{w=1}^{4} E_w} \qquad \text{not, in general,} \qquad \frac{1}{4}\sum_{w=1}^{4} \frac{O_w}{E_w}

Symbols and pronunciation

  • w w (say "double-u"): week number, from 1 to 4

  • Ow O_w (say "oh sub double-u"): on-time deliveries in week w w

  • Ew E_w (say "ee sub double-u"): eligible deliveries in week w w

Inputs and assumptions

Weekly qualifying and eligible counts built under one unchanged KPI definition.

Worked steps

  1. Step 1: Add the on-time counts: 420+438+425+392=1,675 420 + 438 + 425 + 392 = 1{,}675 .

  2. Step 2: Add the eligible counts: 500×4=2,000 500 \times 4 = 2{,}000 .

  3. Step 3: Divide once: 1,675/2,000=0.8375 1{,}675 / 2{,}000 = 0.8375 , or 83.75%.

Worked result

Four-week on-time rate = 83.75%, a gap of −1.25 percentage points against 85.0%.

What the result means

Each eligible delivery carries equal weight. The right-hand expression gives each week equal weight instead. The two coincide here only because every Ew E_w equals 500. With 100 and 400 deliveries, they give 82.5% and 78.0%.

When to use it

Use count-first aggregation for any overall rate built from subgroups: weeks, regions or channels.

Limits and conditions

The pooled rate hides differences between the subgroups. Report the subgroup rows alongside it.

How to check the reference

In SPSS Block H2, AGGREGATE sums the counts and lists overall_rate .8375; Slide_Practice!B34 should show 83.75%.

📖 Key terms

Key terms

KPI Specification: The written facts that let another analyst reproduce the same measure: purpose, unit, population, window, grain, eligibility, calculation, direction, benchmark and refresh schedule.
Eligible Population: The records allowed into a KPI's denominator under its rules.
Count-First Aggregation: Summing qualifying and eligible counts across subgroups before dividing once.
Delivery-Weighted Rate: An overall rate in which each delivery carries equal influence.
Week-Weighted Average: An average of weekly rates in which each week carries equal influence regardless of volume.
✅ Study check

Put the learning into action

  • Write a complete KPI specification before calculating, and keep it beside the result.

  • Build overall rates by summing counts first, and show the subgroup rows beside the total.

  • Treat any change in eligibility, window or threshold as a new KPI version and disclose it.

Center and Position: Describing Late Deliveries

🔍 Go deeper

Why a Rate Needs Center and Position

The on-time rate counts how often deliveries were late, not how late they were. To describe severity, the session summarizes late minutes among late deliveries. The mean is the total divided by the count and uses every value. The median is the ordered middle value, or the average of the two middle values when the count is even. A percentile is a position statement: the 90th percentile is a threshold at or below which about 90% of values fall, under a stated convention. Mean and median describe center; the percentile describes position.

Concept

How the Three Summaries Respond to Long Delays

The mean adds every value, so a few long delays pull it upward. The median depends on the middle positions and moves much less. The 90th percentile sits in the upper part of the ordered values and shows how long the longer delays are. A mean above the median can be consistent with a right-skewed distribution, one with a longer tail of high values, but the session treats this only as a prompt to inspect the distribution. Percentiles depend on a convention: the lab uses Excel's PERCENTILE.INC, and SPSS's rule can differ slightly.

🧮 Worked example

Worked Evidence: Late Minutes in the Latest Week

In the week of August 24, 108 of 500 eligible deliveries were late. The session reports a mean of 12.4 minutes, a median of 7 and a 90th percentile of 31. To make these traceable, this toolkit tabulated late_minutes for those 108 rows of orders_story.csv (week_start 2026-08-24, eligible, late_minutes above 0). Every promised time is 45 minutes, and late_minutes is delivered time minus 45. The total is 1,339.2 minutes, and 1,339.2 ÷ 108 = 12.4.

Worked evidence

Population: 108 late eligible deliveries in the latest week (computed from orders_story.csv)

Period: August 24 through August 30, 2026

Unit: Minutes late per delivery

Minutes late Deliveries Sorted positions Minutes contributed
2.0 20 1 to 20 40.0
7.0 35 21 to 55 245.0
12.0 41 56 to 96 492.0
31.0 2 97 to 98 62.0
50.0 9 99 to 107 450.0
50.2 1 108 50.2

Interpretation: Most late deliveries were 2 to 12 minutes late, but ten were about 50 minutes late, which lifts the mean well above the median.

Concept

Interpreting the Mean, Median, and 90th Percentile

With 108 values, the median averages the 54th and 55th sorted values; both are 7, so half the late deliveries were 7 minutes late or less. The mean, 12.4, is 5.4 minutes higher because ten deliveries were about 50 minutes late. The 90th percentile, 31 minutes, places the upper end of severity near half an hour; repeated values mean the split need not be exactly 90/10. The median describes the typical late experience, the mean the average burden, and the percentile the longer delays. Together they justify inspecting the full distribution in Session 3, not a conclusion about causes.

⚠️ Common mistake

Common Misconception: One Summary Tells the Whole Story

A frequent error reports the mean alone as the "typical" delay. Here 96 of the 108 late deliveries were 12 minutes late or less, below the 12.4 mean. The opposite error reports only the reassuring median and hides the ten deliveries near 50 minutes. A third error forgets the subset: these summaries describe the 108 late deliveries in one week, not all 500; across all eligible deliveries the mean late time would be far smaller because 392 contribute zero. State the population, window and subset for every summary.

🚧 Limits and conditions

Limits of Center and Position Summaries

Three numbers cannot show whether long delays clustered on certain days, regions or weekends, and they cannot identify a cause. Percentiles vary by software convention, especially with repeated values and small groups. The session reserves claims about skew, outliers, spread and shape for Session 3. Choose the form by the decision: a mean when every value's contribution matters, a median or percentile when skew, service thresholds or tail experience matter.

Concept

Mean, Median, and Inclusive Percentile

xˉ=1n∑i=1nxi,x~=x(n/2)+x(n/2+1)2 for even n,positionp=1+p (n−1) \bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i, \qquad \tilde{x} = \frac{x_{(n/2)} + x_{(n/2+1)}}{2} \ \text{for even } n, \qquad \text{position}_{p} = 1 + p\,(n-1)

Symbols and pronunciation

  • xˉ \bar{x} (say "x-bar"): mean late minutes

  • x~ \tilde{x} (say "x-tilde"): median late minutes

  • n n (say "en"): number of late deliveries, here 108

  • x(k) x_{(k)} : the value at sorted position k k

  • p p : the percentile as a proportion, here 0.9

Inputs and assumptions

Late minutes for eligible late deliveries in one week, sorted from smallest to largest.

Worked steps

  1. Step 1: Mean: 1,339.2/108=12.4 1{,}339.2 / 108 = 12.4 minutes.

  2. Step 2: Median: n=108 n = 108 is even, so average positions 54 and 55: (7+7)/2=7 (7 + 7) / 2 = 7 minutes.

  3. Step 3: 90th percentile position: 1+0.9×107=97.3 1 + 0.9 \times 107 = 97.3 , between positions 97 and 98.

  4. Step 4: Both positions hold 31, so the 90th percentile is 31 minutes.

Worked result

Mean 12.4 minutes; median 7 minutes; 90th percentile 31 minutes.

What the result means

The position rule shown is the inclusive rule used by Excel's PERCENTILE.INC. Other rules interpolate differently and can give slightly different cut points. The median needs only the middle positions; the mean needs every value.

When to use it

When a KPI must describe how severe a problem was, not just how often it occurred.

Limits and conditions

These summaries describe the observed late deliveries only. They do not establish skew, outliers or causes without inspecting the full distribution.

How to check the reference

KPI_Build!D18:F18 should show 12.4, 7 and 31. In SPSS, Guided Step 2 runs EXAMINE on the same 108 deliveries; its percentile rule may differ slightly from 31.

📖 Key terms

Key terms

Mean: The sum of eligible numerical values divided by their count; every magnitude affects it.
Median: The ordered middle value, or the average of the two middle values when the count is even.
Percentile: A threshold describing position in an ordered distribution under a stated convention.
Right-Skewed: Describes a distribution with a longer tail of high values; a mean above the median is consistent with it but does not prove it.
Late Minutes: Delivered time minus promised time for a late delivery; zero for an on-time delivery in this file.
✅ Study check

Put the learning into action

  • Pair a frequency KPI such as the on-time rate with a severity summary such as the median or 90th percentile of late minutes.

  • State the population, window, subset and percentile convention beside every center or position summary.

  • Treat a mean well above the median as a reason to inspect the distribution, not as a finding.

MetroMeal's four weeks

Learning goals

  • Distinguish variables from observations and classify each field separately by data type and measurement scale.

  • Identify the grain of raw and aggregated tables, test a candidate key, and explain how changing grain changes the supported claim.

  • Detect the mixed-grain error created by a one-to-many join and restore the correct grain before calculating a KPI.

Variables, Observations, Data Types, and Measurement Scales

Concept

Variables and Observations

A variable is a characteristic recorded for members or events, such as region or delivery minutes; it appears as a column. An observation is the set of values for one member or event; it appears as a row. Cross-sectional data describe many entities at one period; time-series data track a measure through ordered periods. MetroMeal's weekly table is a four-point time series, too short to establish a stable trend. A dataset can contain every eligible event in its window and still not represent future periods, excluded events or a broader customer population.

Concept

Data Type Versus Measurement Scale

Each field receives two classifications. Data type: categorical (labels, codes, flags) or numerical, which is discrete when counted and continuous when measured. Measurement scale: nominal (names, no order), ordinal (ordered, unknown spacing), interval (equal gaps, no true zero) or ratio (equal gaps and a true zero, so ratios make sense). Storage format is a third, unrelated property: digits stored as numbers do not make a field numerical. The session's analogy: jersey number 10 is not twice jersey number 5.

🧮 Worked example

Worked Evidence: One MetroMeal Observation

Order 10482 appears in the slides and in orders_story.csv. Reading across its row gives one observation: customer 5241, completed Saturday, August 8, 2026 (week starting August 3), North region, 3 items, promised 45 minutes, delivered in 54, 9 minutes late, satisfaction category 2, eligible, not on time, no complaint. Completion date is a date-time variable: ordered and usable for interval calculations under defined conventions, but not an ordinary quantity just because Excel stores it as a number.

Worked evidence

Population: Fields in the MetroMeal delivery file (orders_story.csv)

Period: August 3 through August 30, 2026

Unit: One field per row of this table

Field Order 10482 value Data type Measurement scale Analytical role
order_id 10482 Categorical Nominal Identifier (candidate key)
region North Categorical Nominal Category
satisfaction_category 2 Categorical Ordinal Ordered category
item_count 3 Numerical, discrete Ratio Measure
delivery_minutes 54.0 Numerical, continuous Ratio Measure
on_time_kpi_flag 0 Categorical (binary) Nominal Flag

Interpretation: Digits appear in order_id, satisfaction_category and item_count, but only item_count and delivery_minutes support ordinary arithmetic.

Concept

Interpreting the Classifications

Classification decides which summaries are meaningful. An average of order_id values means nothing. For satisfaction_category, 2 is lower than 4, but the gap from 1 to 2 need not equal the gap from 4 to 5, so use counts, category percentages and the median. In the file the categories run 1: 47, 2: 278, 3: 557, 4: 560 and 5: 558 deliveries (counted from orders_story.csv). For item_count and delivery_minutes, a true zero exists, so sums, means and ratios work. A 0/1 flag is categorical, yet summing it counts the 1s and averaging it gives their proportion.

⚠️ Common mistake

Common Misconception: If Excel Can Average It, It Is a Number

Excel will average any column of digits, but that does not make the result meaningful: averaged order IDs, postal codes or ordinal codes have no interpretation. A related error mixes the classifications: "nominal" is a scale, "discrete" is a type, so item_count is numerical discrete and ratio-scaled. A third error treats ordinal ratings as equally spaced by default. A mean rating needs an explicitly disclosed equal-interval convention plus the category frequencies, because a mean alone can hide a split between very satisfied and very dissatisfied customers. Store identifiers as Text so formulas do not treat labels as quantities.

🚧 Limits and conditions

Limits of Classification

Some classifications belong to the construct; others depend on the analytical use. Recorded precision does not settle type: minutes recorded as whole numbers still measure continuous time. Dates need explicit conventions before subtraction. Classification tells you which operations are admissible, not whether values are accurate or complete; that is Session 3's work.

Concept

Summing and Averaging a 0/1 Flag

E=∑i=1Nfi,1E∑i∈eligiblegi=OE E = \sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i, \qquad \frac{1}{E}\sum_{i \in \text{eligible}} g_i = \frac{O}{E}

Symbols and pronunciation

  • N N (say "en"): rows in the Orders table, here 2,000

  • fi f_i (say "f sub i"): eligible_kpi_flag for row i i , either 0 or 1

  • gi g_i (say "g sub i"): on_time_kpi_flag for row i i , either 0 or 1

  • E E and O O : eligible and on-time counts

Inputs and assumptions

Flags coded 1 when the condition is true and 0 otherwise, with no blanks.

Worked steps

  1. Step 1: Sum eligible_kpi_flag over all rows: E=2,000 E = 2{,}000 (KPI_Build!B5).

  2. Step 2: Within the latest week, sum on_time_kpi_flag among eligible rows: O=392 O = 392 .

  3. Step 3: Divide by the week's eligible count: 392/500=0.784 392 / 500 = 0.784 .

Worked result

The sum of a flag is a count; the average of a flag over eligible rows is the proportion of 1s.

What the result means

This is why a nominal 0/1 field can still feed a KPI. The arithmetic is on the coded condition, not on a measured quantity.

When to use it

Counting eligible, on-time or complaint deliveries with SUM, SUMIFS or a PivotTable Average.

Limits and conditions

A blank or a code other than 0 and 1 breaks the logic; check the flag's values first.

How to check the reference

In SPSS Guided Step 1, FREQUENCIES on eligible_kpi_flag should show 2,000 cases coded 1.

📖 Key terms

Key terms

Variable: A recorded characteristic, represented by a column.
Observation: One complete row of values for one member or event at the stated grain.
Data Type: Whether values are categorical or numerical, and whether numerical values are discrete or continuous.
Measurement Scale: Whether a field is nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio in meaning.
Identifier: A code that names an entity or event; arithmetic on it has no useful meaning.
✅ Study check

Put the learning into action

  • Classify every field twice, by data type and by measurement scale, in separate columns.

  • Check whether arithmetic is meaningful before averaging any field that software stores as a number.

  • Summarize ordinal ratings with frequencies and the median, and disclose any equal-interval convention.

Row Grain, Candidate Keys, and Mixed-Grain Join Risk

Concept

What Grain Means

Grain is the meaning of one row: its entity or event, level of detail and time unit. The grain test is to complete "Each row represents one ..."; more than one incompatible ending signals mixed grain. A candidate key is a field, or combination of fields, that is unique at the stated grain. MetroMeal's raw table has one row per eligible completed delivery, keyed by order_id; its weekly summary has one row per week. Delivery rows support checks on individual orders and exceptions; weekly rows support comparisons across weeks.

Concept

How a One-to-Many Join Changes Weight

In a one-to-many join, one parent row matches several child rows. Joining orders (one row per order) to items (one row per item) yields one row per item, repeating each order once per item. The session calls this the join fan trap: parents receive unequal weight. Repeated order IDs after the join are expected at item grain, not corrupt data; the error is computing an order-level measure on the joined rows. The repair is to aggregate the child table to one row per order first, then verify key, relationship and row count before using COUNT or AVERAGE.

🧮 Worked example

Worked Evidence: Two Orders, Four Rows

The session's illustration uses Order A, late with three items, and Order B, on time with one item. At order grain the on-time rate is 1 ÷ 2 = 50.0%. After joining the item table, A appears three times and B once, so a row-based rate reports 1 ÷ 4 = 25.0%. Nothing about delivery changed; the late order simply received triple weight. SPSS Block H3 uses the same structure and aggregates the four item rows back to two orders.

Worked evidence

Population: Two-order teaching illustration (not the MetroMeal file)

Period: Not applicable; structural example

Unit: Item rows after the join

Joined row order_id item_id Order outcome Counted as
1 A I1 Late Late row
2 A I2 Late Late row
3 A I3 Late Late row
4 B I4 On time On-time row

Interpretation: Four joined rows contain only two distinct orders, so the row-based rate of 25.0% misstates the order-level rate of 50.0%.

Concept

Interpreting Grain in the MetroMeal File

The MetroMeal file passes its grain test: ROWS(Orders[order_id]) and ROWS(UNIQUE(Orders[order_id])) both return 2,000, so order_id is unique at delivery grain, and SUM(Orders[eligible_kpi_flag]) returns 2,000. The file also shows why a join would matter: 1,675 deliveries have one item and 325 have three (from item_count), so a direct join to an item table would create 1,675 + 3 × 325 = 2,650 rows and count multi-item deliveries three times. Aggregation runs the other way: 500 delivery rows become one weekly row that cannot be taken apart again.

⚠️ Common mistake

Common Misconception: Deleting Repeats Cleans the Table

Seeing repeated order_id values after a join, analysts often delete the "duplicates". At item grain the repeats are correct; deleting rows loses information and may keep the wrong outcome. Decide which grain the question needs, then aggregate, for example with MAX of an order-level flag and a count of item rows, as Block H3 does. The opposite error treats four joined rows as four orders, quietly giving customers who buy more items more say. In a table that should be at order grain, duplicate keys need investigation before deletion: they may be errors or evidence that the assumed grain is wrong.

🚧 Limits and conditions

Limits of the Grain Test

Matching row and distinct-key counts shows the key is unique, not that every row is real and eligible or that nothing is missing. A correctly stated grain may still not suit the question: a line-item defect decision needs item grain with a redefined population and denominator. Aggregated tables cannot support claims about individual deliveries. Use raw grain to validate records and weekly grain for weekly decisions.

Predict the rows after joining every item to its order, state each table's grain, choose the safe grain for the KPI, and explain what goes wrong on the joined rows. Whose experience gets extra weight? Check: 310 joined rows, one per item; the KPI needs one row per order.

Optional independent practice: my response

Write your approach, supporting evidence and assumptions here. After checking the explanation, record what you would revise.
Concept

Key Test and Joined-Row Count

Nrows=Ndistinct ⇒ key is unique at this grain,njoined=∑j=1mkj N_{\text{rows}} = N_{\text{distinct}} \ \Rightarrow \ \text{key is unique at this grain}, \qquad n_{\text{joined}} = \sum_{j=1}^{m} k_j

Symbols and pronunciation

  • Nrows N_{\text{rows}} : number of rows in the table

  • Ndistinct N_{\text{distinct}} : number of distinct values of the candidate key

  • m m : number of parent orders; kj k_j : number of child item rows for order j j

Inputs and assumptions

A candidate key column, and for joins, the number of matching child rows per parent.

Worked steps

  1. Step 1: MetroMeal: Nrows=2,000 N_{\text{rows}} = 2{,}000 and Ndistinct=2,000 N_{\text{distinct}} = 2{,}000 , so order_id is unique at delivery grain.

  2. Step 2: Two-order illustration: kA=3 k_A = 3 and kB=1 k_B = 1 , so njoined=4 n_{\text{joined}} = 4 .

  3. Step 3: Row-based on-time rate after the join: 1/4=25.0% 1 / 4 = 25.0\% ; order-level rate: 1/2=50.0% 1 / 2 = 50.0\% .

Worked result

The key test passes for MetroMeal; the join multiplies Order A's weight by three.

What the result means

Equal counts mean no key value repeats. After a one-to-many join, the row count equals the number of child rows, so row-based rates weight parents by their number of children.

When to use it

Before any COUNT, AVERAGE or rate on a table that came from a join.

Limits and conditions

A passing key test does not prove completeness or correct eligibility.

How to check the reference

KPI_Build!B3 and B4 both show 2000. In SPSS Guided Step 1, AGGREGATE by order_id produces rows_per_order with minimum and maximum 1.

📖 Key terms

Key terms

Grain: What one row represents: its entity or event, level of detail and time unit.
Candidate Key: A field or combination of fields that is unique at the stated grain.
One-to-Many Join: A join where one row in one table matches several rows in another.
Join Fan Trap: The reweighting that occurs when parent rows are repeated for each matching child row.
Mixed-Grain Risk: The distortion that occurs when repeated entities change their analytical weight in a summary.
✅ Study check

Put the learning into action

  • Complete the grain sentence for every table before calculating anything.

  • Test the candidate key by comparing row and distinct-key counts.

  • Aggregate child tables to the grain the KPI needs before joining or calculating a rate.

Concept

Complete the sentence

Key test

The Join Fan Trap

2.4 · Honest Charts, Bounded Stories, and Validation

In classSlides 55–70

Practise it in the lab
  • Part G: Does the chart communicate honestly? · 3 min
  • Part H: What makes the MetroMeal dashboard chart misleading? · 3 min · SPSS Block H4: four weekly rates and a simple zero-baseline bar chart
  • Part I: Is the data story traceable and bounded? · 3 min
  • Part J: Can every number in the MetroMeal story be traced? · 3 min · SPSS Block H5: reconcile the latest evidence and calculate story values
  • Part M: Does the chart show the checked numbers honestly? · 4 min · SPSS Guided Step 3: weekly on-time chart from checked values

About 16 min read · PDF pages 45–58 · Short version (Concise)

Learning goals

  • Select a table, bar chart or line chart according to the viewer's question, and critique a chart for baseline, denominator, color, clutter and title problems.

  • Repair a misleading chart so that it shows checked values with a zero baseline, direct labels, denominators, a target line and a non-color cue.

  • Write a three-sentence bounded story and validate every number in it through an independent route.

Chart Selection, Baselines, and Accessible Critique

Concept

Matching the Display to the Question

Choose the display by the viewer's task. A table supports exact lookup, a bar chart compares magnitudes across categories or periods, and a line chart emphasizes ordered progression. Horizontal bars suit long labels; order categories naturally or by a disclosed rule; never connect unordered categories with lines. Match the statistic too: a weekly rate is a proportion with a denominator, not a count or a causal effect, and a target line is a benchmark, not a fitted average. Show counts and rates together when a changing denominator could explain a rate movement.

Concept

How Baselines, Clutter, and Accessibility Shape Perception

Viewers judge bars by length from a common baseline, so quantitative bar charts should begin at zero; a truncated axis makes modest differences look large. Line charts encode position and may use a narrower range when the range, labels and context are explicit. Clutter is decoration, unneeded gridlines, redundant labels, 3D effects and excess color. Emphasis should direct attention to a decision-relevant feature without hiding context. Accessible charts use readable text, contrast, direct labels and cues beyond color, with a text description and data table.

🧮 Worked example

Worked Evidence: Critiquing and Repairing Chart A

The session's Chart A shows MetroMeal's four weekly rates as 3D bars on a 75% to 90% axis, uses red and green as the only status cues, omits denominators and is titled "Delivery performance collapses." The critique protocol checks meaning first (decision, statistic, grain, period, eligibility, numerator, denominator, source), then encoding and accessibility, then whether the title matches the data. The repair uses a zero baseline, direct labels, a labeled 85% target, one accessible emphasis on the latest week and visible denominators.

Worked evidence

Population: MetroMeal weekly on-time rates, 500 eligible deliveries per week

Period: August 3 through August 30, 2026

Unit: Chart features

Feature Chart A (flawed) Repaired chart
Axis 75.0% to 90.0% 0.0% to 100.0%
Form 3D vertical bars 2D bars with an 85.0% target line
Denominators Omitted Label "78.4% (n = 500)" on each bar
Status cue Red and green only Pattern fill or thick outline on the latest bar
Title "Delivery performance collapses." "Week of August 24 on-time delivery was 78.4%, 6.6 percentage points below target."

Interpretation: The data values are identical in both charts; only the encoding and wording change what a reader believes.

Concept

Interpreting the Repaired Chart

On the truncated axis, the 78.4% bar occupies only 3.4 points of a 15-point range and looks close to collapse. On a 0% to 100% axis it sits 9.2 points below the 87.6% week and 6.6 points below target: concerning, but far from zero. The repaired chart supports a bounded reading: the latest observed week was lower than each prior week and below target, with each rate resting on 500 deliveries. It does not show why, establish a trend from four points or forecast next week.

⚠️ Common mistake

Common Misconception: Cosmetic Cleanup Is a Repair

Fixing the colors while keeping the 75.0% baseline is not a repair; the bars still exaggerate the dip. Typing rates into the chart table instead of linking them is another error: a later correction leaves the chart disagreeing with the analysis. Reading counts as rates is a third: in the lab's RiverTown case, 54 of 60 is the same 90.0% as 72 of 80, although 54 looks smaller. Finally, zero is not required for every chart; a clearly labeled line chart may use a narrower range.

🚧 Limits and conditions

Limits of Chart Repair

An honest chart cannot repair a wrong eligibility rule, grain or denominator; it only displays the error clearly. Emphasis always carries a message, so ask whether highlighting the latest week is warranted or merely dramatic. If a repair changes the apparent story, revise the claim rather than keeping dramatic wording. A chart read without a presenter needs its own title, labels, annotation, source and limitation.

🧭 Guided practice

Guided Practice: Is RiverTown's Chart Honest?

RiverTown is a made-up program from Lab Part G: attendance was 72 of 80 eligible residents in January, 54 of 60 in February and 30 of 50 in March, against an 85.0% target. The flawed chart starts at 50.0% and uses red and green alone. Task 1: Calculate the three rates. Task 2: Name the scale or denominator problem and the color-only problem. Task 3: List the repairs. Task 4: Write a title stating the observed March comparison without "will". Check: 90.0%, 90.0%, 60.0%.

Changed-Case Transfer: A Line Chart for the Same Weeks

Suppose the director's question is about sequence rather than magnitude. Design a line chart of MetroMeal's four weekly rates. Decide whether a nonzero range is acceptable and which labels, target line and window disclosure are required. Explain what the line emphasizes that bars do not, and write one sentence on why four connected points do not establish a stable trend.

Optional independent practice: my response

Write your approach, supporting evidence and assumptions here. After checking the explanation, record what you would revise.
Concept

How a Truncated Axis Distorts Bar Length

visible share=v−amin⁡amax⁡−amin⁡,apparent ratio=v1−amin⁡v2−amin⁡ \text{visible share} = \frac{v - a_{\min}}{a_{\max} - a_{\min}}, \qquad \text{apparent ratio} = \frac{v_1 - a_{\min}}{v_2 - a_{\min}}

Symbols and pronunciation

  • v v : plotted value, such as 0.784

  • amin⁡ a_{\min} and amax⁡ a_{\max} (say "a-min" and "a-max"): the lowest and highest values on the axis

  • v1 v_1 and v2 v_2 : two plotted values being compared

Inputs and assumptions

A bar chart whose bar length starts at the axis minimum.

Worked steps

  1. Step 1: Truncated axis, 75% to 90%: the 78.4% bar fills (78.4−75)/15=22.7% (78.4 - 75) / 15 = 22.7\% of the plot height; the 87.6% bar fills (87.6−75)/15=84.0% (87.6 - 75) / 15 = 84.0\% .

  2. Step 2: Apparent ratio of the two bars: 12.6/3.4=3.7 12.6 / 3.4 = 3.7 , so one bar looks almost four times the other.

  3. Step 3: Zero baseline: 87.6/78.4=1.12 87.6 / 78.4 = 1.12 , so the bars differ by about 12%, matching the data.

Worked result

Truncation turns a 9.2-point difference into bars that look 3.7 times different in length.

What the result means

Above a zero minimum, bar length no longer represents the value, so the eye reads a false ratio.

When to use it

To explain why a dashboard axis must be reset before a decision.

Limits and conditions

The calculation applies to length encodings such as bars. Line charts encode position and can use narrower ranges with clear labels.

How to check the reference

In Chart_Build, set the vertical axis to Minimum 0 and Maximum 1, then compare the bar lengths with the Step 3 ratio.

📖 Key terms

Key terms

Truncated Axis: A quantitative axis that starts above zero, distorting bar length.
Baseline: The reference from which bar length is judged, normally zero.
Clutter: Visual elements that consume attention without adding evidence.
Direct Label: A value written on or beside the data mark instead of in a separate legend.
Non-Color Cue: A pattern, outline, label or position that carries meaning without relying on color.
✅ Study check

Put the learning into action

  • Choose a table, bar or line by the viewer's task and the statistic being shown.

  • Apply the critique protocol: meaning and denominator first, then encoding and accessibility, then the title.

  • Build charts from linked, checked cells with a zero baseline, direct labels, denominators and a non-color cue.

Bounded Data Stories and Independent Validation

Concept

From Exploratory Analysis to an Explanatory Story

Exploratory analysis searches across possible patterns, questions and data issues. Explanatory communication selects checked evidence for a defined audience and decision; purpose, not polish, is the difference. A bounded story says only what the records support, linking audience and decision, observed result, comparison, bounded action, limitation and next check. An explanatory title states the supported takeaway, and an annotation adds decision context rather than repeating a label.

Concept

How Claim Verbs and Validation Work

The strongest verb sets the evidence standard. "Observed" reports a value; "lower than" compares; "associated with" notes co-occurrence; "predicts" needs testing on new outcomes; "caused" needs evidence that changing one factor changed another after other explanations were ruled out. Four descriptive weeks support the first three. Validation challenges a result independently: reconcile counts, inspect records, recalculate by a second route and compare labels, cells and narrative. Re-entering the same formula checks arithmetic only. The traceability chain runs from decision to grain, KPI, statistic, chart, claim, action, limitation and next check.

🧮 Worked example

Worked Evidence: Validating the MetroMeal Story

The session's model story: "For the operations director deciding whether to investigate weekend staffing before the next schedule, on-time delivery for August 24 through August 30 was 78.4%, or 392 of 500 eligible deliveries. This was 6.6 percentage points below the 85% target and lower than the prior three observed weeks, which ranged from 84.0% to 87.6%. The complaint rate remained within its 3% guardrail at 2.8%. Review order-level timing by day and relevant staffing records before reallocating resources because four descriptive weeks do not establish the cause or the likely effect of a staffing change." Each number is checked below.

Worked evidence

Population: Eligible completed MetroMeal deliveries

Period: August 3 through August 30, 2026

Unit: Story phrases and their checks

Story phrase Source cell Independent check Result
392 of 500 KPI_Build!D10, C10 392 + 108 − 500 0
78.4% KPI_Build!E10 392 ÷ 500 by hand; SPSS H5 0.784
6.6 points below KPI_Build!F10 85.0 − 78.4 6.6
84.0% to 87.6% KPI_Build!E7:E9 420 ÷ 500 and 438 ÷ 500 84.0%, 87.6%
2.8% KPI_Build!H10 14 ÷ 500 by hand 0.028

Interpretation: Every number traces to a checked cell and a second route, and the final sentence names the causal limit.

Concept

Interpreting an Exploratory Clue Without Overclaiming

The lab's optional Topic 2 splits weeks by weekend_flag. In the latest week, 320 of 358 weekday deliveries (89.4%) and 72 of 142 weekend deliveries (50.7%) were on time. Computed the same way from orders_story.csv, earlier weekend rates were 97 of 142 (68.3%), 102 of 142 (71.8%) and 97 of 142 (68.3%). This exploratory observation strengthens the case for investigating weekend operations, but weather, restaurant delays, demand, routes and order mix may also differ on weekends. A bounded sentence: "In the week of August 24, the weekend on-time rate was 50.7% (72 of 142), compared with 89.4% on weekdays; weekend staffing is one hypothesis to investigate, not an established cause."

⚠️ Common mistake

Common Misconception: A Real Miss Proves the Cause

The most common story error keeps a causal sentence because the rate really did miss the target. A real miss does not reveal its cause. "Weekend understaffing caused a delivery crisis" adds an undefined dramatic word to a causal verb; the session asks writers to remove "collapse", "crisis", "significant", "caused" and "will" unless supported. A row of Self_Check ticks is not proof either: it compares numbers and counts words, and cannot detect a causal claim. Avoid generic limits such as "More research is needed"; write "Four descriptive weeks do not identify the cause or expected effect of a staffing change."

🚧 Limits and conditions

Limits of a Bounded Story and the Bridge to Session 3

A bounded story is only as reliable as its data. If table, formula, chart and narrative disagree, stop and resolve the difference before recommending action. The session's forward-check list for Session 3 covers missing completion times, duplicate order identifiers, changed eligibility, unusual delays and whether mean, median, spread and shape agree. If missing records were disproportionately late, the true rate would be lower. Generalizing beyond the window needs later sampling methods, and a causal claim would need credible variation in staffing, aligned comparison periods, reliable scheduling records and checks for other explanations.

🧭 Guided practice

Guided Practice: Is GreenBlock's Story Bounded?

GreenBlock is a made-up organization from Lab Part I. Over three observed months, 273 of 300 eligible repairs were completed within the service window, against a 95.0% target, and a draft claims a new policy caused the miss. Task 1: Calculate the rate and the gap in points. Task 2: Separate what the records show from what the draft claims. Task 3: Write a bounded title, an action (investigate before revising) and a limitation naming the three-month scope. Task 4: Write exactly three sentences. Check: 91.0% and −4.0 points.

🔁 Transfer

Changed-Case Transfer: Two Audiences, One Set of Facts

Adapt the MetroMeal story for two readers. The executive version leads with the target miss and the investigation decision; the analyst version adds the 392 of 500 denominator, the KPI definition, source checks and the four-week limitation. A circulated document, unlike a live talk, must carry definitions, labels, denominators, window and limits on the page. List what changed between versions and what could not change: facts, units and causal boundaries.

Optional independent practice: my response

Write your approach, supporting evidence and assumptions here. After checking the explanation, record what you would revise.
Concept

Reconciliation Identity

O+L−E=0,OE+LE=1 O + L - E = 0, \qquad \frac{O}{E} + \frac{L}{E} = 1

Symbols and pronunciation
  • O O : on-time eligible deliveries; L L : late eligible deliveries; E E : eligible deliveries
Inputs and assumptions

Every eligible delivery is classified as either on time or late, never both and never neither.

Worked steps

  1. Step 1: Substitute the latest week: 392+108−500=0 392 + 108 - 500 = 0 .

  2. Step 2: Check the complements: 0.784+0.216=1 0.784 + 0.216 = 1 , so the on-time and late rates cover all eligible deliveries.

  3. Step 3: Reach the late count a second way, by counting rows with late_minutes above 0: 108, then confirm KPI_Build!G18 shows 0.

Worked result

The identity holds: 392 + 108 = 500; 78.4% + 21.6% = 100%.

What the result means

A nonzero result would signal missing, duplicated or misclassified records before any rate is reported.

When to use it

Before a number goes into a story, chart title or recommendation.

Limits and conditions

Reconciliation confirms internal consistency. It cannot detect deliveries that never entered the file.

How to check the reference

SPSS Block H5 computes reconcile = ontime + late − eligible and lists 0.

📖 Key terms

Key terms

Exploratory Analysis: A broad search for possible patterns, questions and data issues.
Explanatory Communication: Selected, checked evidence presented for a defined audience and decision.
Bounded Claim: A statement limited to the observed population, period, comparison and design.
Causal Claim: A statement that one factor produced an outcome; it requires evidence that isolates the proposed cause.
Independent Validation: A challenge to a result through reconciliation, source inspection, a second calculation route or comparison across artifacts.
✅ Study check

Put the learning into action

  • Draft a story with the five-part frame before formatting any chart.

  • Trace every quantitative phrase to a checked cell and verify at least one number by a second route.

  • Underline the strongest verb in each sentence and confirm that the evidence supports it.

📌 Reference summary

Reference summary

Use these concise reminders after reading the complete explanations above.

Concept

Choose the Display

Task decides form
  • Table for exact lookup, bars for magnitude comparison, lines for ordered sequence.
Match the statistic
  • A weekly rate is a proportion with a denominator; a target line is a benchmark, not a fitted value.
Concept

Repair the Chart

Five repairs
  • 0% to 100% bar axis, direct labels with n, 85.0% target line, non-color cue on the latest week, and a title quoting checked values.
Why zero matters
  • On a 75% to 90% axis, 78.4% and 87.6% bars look 3.7 times different; on a zero axis they differ by about 12%.
Concept

Write the Bounded Story

Three sentences
  • What the evidence shows; what it does not show; what the director should do next.
Verbs
  • Use "observed", "lower than" and "warrants investigation". Avoid "caused", "collapse" and "will" without supporting evidence.
Concept

Validate Independently

Reconcile and recompute
  • 392 + 108 − 500 = 0; 392 ÷ 500 = 78.4%; 85.0 − 78.4 = 6.6 points; 14 ÷ 500 = 2.8%.
Compare artifacts
  • Chart labels, table cells and story numbers must agree before the story is shared.

Industry Practice

Use these explanations alongside Appendix C in the student slides. The figures are those reported in the session materials; the teaching inferences are labeled separately.

Slide 105: United States Department of Transportation

A cancellation rate and its reporting scope

  • Reported: 16.3 million flights and a 2023 cancellation rate below 1.2%, fewer than 1.2 cancellations per 100 covered flights.
  • Teaching inference: the rate covers the reported system for the year, not every airline, route or month, and it does not show that any policy caused it.

Source: Session 02 student slides, Appendix C, slide 105.

Slide 106: United Parcel Service

Scale is not service quality

  • Reported: 91.1 billion US dollars in 2024 revenue, 5.7 billion delivered packages and about 22.4 million packages per day.
  • Teaching inference: dollars, package counts and daily averages measure scale in different units; none shows on-time performance, and a daily average can hide peaks.

Source: Session 02 student slides, Appendix C, slide 106.

Slide 107: Netflix Advertising

Absolute change, relative change and the counted unit

  • Reported: advertising-plan monthly active users rose from 40 million in May 2024 to 70 million in November 2024.
  • Teaching inference: the increase is 30 million users, or 30 ÷ 40 = 75% relative growth, not 30 percentage points; a monthly active user is not automatically a paying account.

Source: Session 02 student slides, Appendix C, slide 107.

Slide 108: Wells Fargo and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau

Accounts, customers and amounts are different units

  • Reported: over 2 billion US dollars in customer redress and a 1.7 billion US dollar civil penalty, covering more than 16 million accounts.
  • Teaching inference: an account is not a unique customer or incident, and redress (to consumers) differs from a penalty (to the government), so redress per account can hide unequal harm.

Source: Session 02 student slides, Appendix C, slide 108.
